opus-5.5.text:
Well, thank you for having me. You know, I've been thinking about this for a long time, really since the early days of ImageNet. When we started working on visual intelligence, the field was focused on helping computers *see*: recognize objects, label images. But seeing is just the beginning. If you look at how intelligence evolved in animals, vision came about over half a billion years ago, and it didn't evolve just so creatures could name things. It evolved so they could move, navigate, manipulate, survive in a three-dimensional world. Perception and action are deeply intertwined, and all of that happens in 3D space.

Language models have been incredibly powerful, and I'm genuinely excited about what they've done. But language is fundamentally a one-dimensional, sequential signal, and it's a human-generated abstraction. The physical world isn't like that. The world is 3D, it obeys physics, things have geometry, occlusion, depth, material properties. You can't fully capture that by predicting the next token, or even by generating flat 2D pixels. If we want machines that can truly understand and interact with the world the way we do, they need to reason in the native structure of that world.

That's what I call spatial intelligence, and I think it's one of the most important frontiers in AI right now. At World Labs, building world models that are fundamentally 3D means a model that can perceive a scene, reconstruct it, generate new worlds, and let you, or an agent, move through them and reason about them consistently. Not just a pretty video that falls apart when you turn the camera, but a world with persistence and coherence.

And the applications are enormous. Think about creators, game designers, filmmakers, architects, who could build and iterate on rich 3D environments in a fraction of the time. Think about robotics, where the bottleneck is often understanding and simulating the physical world. Think about AR and VR, design, education, even healthcare. All of these depend on understanding space.

So for me, it's not a side problem. I really believe that, alongside language, spatial intelligence is one of the pillars of what it means to be intelligent. And it's a hard problem: the data is scarcer, the representations are more complex. But that's exactly why it's worth working on now.

r001.rationale: The response links fundamentally 3D world models to spatial intelligence and describes broad applications—including robotics, games, architecture, AR/VR, education, and healthcare—that depend on understanding space.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. So, I think about this a lot, and I keep coming back to evolution. Language is a wonderful, powerful thing, but it's actually a very recent invention in the history of intelligence. Vision, perception, understanding space and objects and physics, that's been evolving for hundreds of millions of years, since the first trilobites developed the ability to sense light. Animals didn't develop language to survive. They developed the ability to perceive and understand and move through a three-dimensional world. That's the foundation on which everything else, including language, was built.

And when I look at where we are right now with AI, large language models have made this incredible leap. But language is fundamentally lossy. It's a compression of the world. If I describe a room to you, I'm giving you a sketch, and your brain is filling in the rest because you've lived in rooms your whole life. A model that only learns from text has never had that experience. It's learning the sketch without ever having seen the thing.

So the question I'm obsessed with is: what does it take to give machines that grounding? To go from pixels, or from a description, to an actual understanding of a world that has geometry, that has objects with permanence, that has physics, where you can move around and things stay consistent. That's what we mean by a world model at World Labs. It's not generating a pretty picture or even a video. It's generating a space you can be in, reason about, and act in.

And I think the applications are enormous. Robotics obviously needs this. A robot cannot operate on language alone. Creators, designers, game developers, architects, people who work in 3D all day, could use tools that actually understand 3D. And honestly, I think it's a step toward a more complete form of intelligence, one that's closer to how we and other living things actually experience the world. Spatial intelligence isn't a niche. It's a missing piece.

r001.rationale: The response says 3D world models could support robotics and a range of creative and design fields, and frames spatial intelligence as a missing piece of AI—communicating broad potential to address spatial intelligence problems.

astra-6.text:
Well, intelligence isn’t just about language. We live in a three-dimensional world, and so much of what we do depends on understanding space: where things are, how they relate to one another, and what might happen when we act. Even something as ordinary as reaching for a cup involves perception, physical reasoning, and action working together.

That’s why I see spatial intelligence as a fundamental problem in AI. An image gives you one view of the world, but the world continues beyond that view. If you move around an object, it should still be the same object. If something is hidden, it hasn’t disappeared. We need models that can capture that underlying structure, rather than only describe what’s visible.

At World Labs, that’s the direction we’re excited about: models that can understand and generate three-dimensional worlds. That could give creators new ways to build and explore, and eventually help machines act more intelligently in physical environments. For me, it’s part of a larger question: how do we build intelligence that understands the world well enough to interact with it?

r001.rationale: The response presents spatial intelligence as fundamental and says 3D world models could help machines act more intelligently, but it does not clearly state that solving the modeling problem could unlock solutions to a broad range of spatial intelligence problems.

sol-6.1.text:
When we look at intelligence, language is only one part of the story. We also perceive the world, understand its structure, and act in it. Even something as simple as picking up a cup requires you to understand space, geometry, and how your actions will change what happens next.

That’s why I think spatial intelligence is such a fundamental problem. A picture gives you one view of the world, but the world doesn’t disappear when you turn your head. A world model needs to capture that underlying structure—to understand how different views relate to the same space, and what can happen within it.

At World Labs, we want to build toward that capability. It opens up possibilities for creating and interacting with virtual worlds, and eventually for helping machines act in the physical world. For me, the exciting question is how we move from AI that can describe things to AI that can understand the worlds those things inhabit.

r001.rationale: The response presents spatial intelligence as a fundamental problem and says the capability could enable virtual-world creation and interaction as well as help machines act in the physical world, communicating a range of spatial applications.
